title: Cap. V Obj. 1 Sol close: distinct decrees still; love unto salvation prepares faith for not-yet-believers
pass_a_gloss: That he might avoid this inconvenience Arminius contends that it is not one decree by which God establishes, I will give life to the faithful, and, I will give faith to this one, but distinct. If they are distinct decrees, why has Arminius himself put both together in the definition of predestination? Further, let them be distinct (about which we labor least) yet since there is a predestination or election of certain persons to faith, it is necessary that this election precede every intuition of faith in the elect; it is necessary that it arise from love destinating to these what is not decreed to others. Finally, since God has elected singular persons to faith, others being passed by, it is plain that he has not done this unaware that this faith would conduce to obtaining eternal life infallibly; but rather that he has ordained and gifted this gift of God to them unto this very end. Love unto salvation has therefore put itself forth toward those not yet believing, by predestinating and preparing for them the gift of faith, by means of which they might believe, and believing enter eternal life. And so you see that this first Arminian objection has no strength.
pass_b_english: To dodge the inconvenience Arminius claims there are not one but distinct decrees — I will give life to the faithful, and I will give faith to this one. If distinct, why did he himself put both in his definition of predestination? Let them be distinct (we care little): still, since there is predestination or election of certain persons to faith, that election must precede every intuition of faith in the elect; it must arise from love destinating to these what is not decreed to others. And when God elects singular persons to faith, others passed by, he does not do it unaware that this faith leads infallibly to eternal life — rather he ordained and gifted them that gift unto that end. So love unto salvation puts itself forth toward not-yet-believers by predestinating and preparing the gift of faith whereby they believe and, believing, enter eternal life. Thus this first Arminian objection has no force.
source_text: Ut hoc incommodum vitaret Arminius, contendit non esse unum decretum quo statuit Deus, Volo fideli dare vitam, et, Volo huic dare fidem, sed distincta. Si sint distincta decreta, cur ipse Arminius in definitionem praedestinationis utrumque confecit? Porro, sint distincta (de quo nos minime laboramus) tamen cum sit praedestinatio sive electio certarum personarum ad fidem, necesse est ut haec electio praecedat omnem fidei intuitum in electis; necesse est ex amore oriatur hisce destinante quod aliis non decernitur. Denique, cum Deus ad fidem elegit singulares personas aliis praeteritis, manifestum est id eum non fecisse inscitum quod haec fides ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter obtinendam conducere; sed hoc potius donum Dei in hunc ipsum finem illis ordinasse et donasse. Exseruit igitur se amor ad salutem erga nondum credentes, praedestinando et praeparando illis donum fidei, quo mediante crederent, credentesque vitam aeternam adirent. Et sic videtis primam hanc objectionem Arminianam nullas vires habere.
